The problem

Educators spend more time structuring content than teaching it.

Building a course from scratch — deciding what modules exist, what topics go in each, what the learning outcomes should be, how assessment maps back to those outcomes — takes weeks. Before a single piece of content is written.

An AI-powered platform could help. The AI could generate module breakdowns, suggest course outcomes mapped to Bloom's taxonomy, draft lesson plans and quizzes. But early versions of Creator Co-Pilot had a trust problem: educators felt like they had lost control of their own course.

The problem wasn't capability. The AI could do everything. The problem was that educators felt like the content was happening to them, not with them.

My brief: design Creator Co-Pilot so that AI assistance feels like having a very capable co-author — one that drafts, suggests, and structures, but never overwrites without permission.

The product
01

Getting started — auth to first course

Login, empty state, and course creation — three screens that set the tone.

Login — Google SSO or email
Clean auth, no friction. Educators arrive ready to work — the sign-in screen doesn't get in the way.
Courses home — Empty state
Empty state with a single clear CTA. No dashboard clutter before there's anything to manage.
Create course — Generate with AI or type
Two options surface immediately: AI-generated full draft from course name, or manual entry. The choice is the educator's.
02

Course dashboard — the full content map

Everything an educator needs to build a course, visible from one screen — without being overwhelmed.

Course dashboard — Introduction to Python
Three sections: Content, Assessment, Documentation. Each item shows current status. Nothing is hidden — the full scope of the course is visible at once.
"Convert to reference" — Compounding AI loop
Generated outcomes can be saved back as a reference — feeding the next generation. Course Outcomes inform Modules, Modules inform Lesson Plans. AI compounds on itself.
03

AI Studio — the generation interface

One interaction model for every content type. Consistent across all 10+ content types.

AI Studio — Generating state
Panel slides in from the right. Prompt bar at bottom. References panel on the right. The generation animation signals activity without blocking the UI.
AI Studio — Results with references visible
Generated content fills the left panel. References stay visible on the right. Educators can verify the AI's source material before accepting any output.
References panel — Select all or individual
"Use reference material only" toggle constrains AI to the educator's own uploads. Select All or pick individual sources — granular control over what the AI draws from.
Resources — Reference library
The reference library that feeds every generation. Uploaded PDFs listed with metadata. The AI's knowledge is bounded by what the educator chooses to include.
AI Studio — Regenerate along a specific direction
Every AI output surfaces contextual regeneration options — Adapt for industry, Increase difficulty, Emphasise theory, Toughen quiz. One tap refines without starting over.
04

Content generation — outcomes, modules, lesson plans

The AI generates structured academic content. The educator retains control at every step.

Course outcomes — AI Studio generating
Same AI Studio layout as every other generation type. One mental model — no relearning required when switching between content types.
Course outcomes — CO1–CO6 with Bloom's taxonomy
Generated outcomes mapped to Bloom's Taxonomy levels and Cognitive Domain. Structured for institutional compliance without requiring educators to know the framework.
Modules & topics — Structured breakdown
8 modules with name, description, intent, and topics. Builds directly from Course Outcomes when used as reference — the AI compounds on previously accepted content.
Lesson plans — 15-day session schedule
High-level session plan: 15 days × 2 sessions. Each session tagged with type (Concept Introduction, Lab, Review). Educators can edit before exporting.
Activities — Module, duration, mode, graded
In-class activities as a structured table. Module-tagged, duration, group/individual, graded flag. Designed for direct export into institutional LMS formats.
05

Assessment generation — quizzes, papers, evaluation

From question banks to full exam papers to student evaluation — format handled by AI, judgement retained by educator.

Quizzes — MCQ with difficulty and Bloom's level
Each question includes options, correct answer, difficulty, and Bloom's taxonomy level. Module-tagged for targeted assessment. Educators review before publishing.
Question papers — CO-mapped exam format
Full question paper with duration, max marks, instructions, and CO mapping per question. Institutionally compliant output without manual formatting effort.
Evaluation — Question paper selection
Evaluation wizard starts with question paper selection. Step 1 of a clear sequence. The wizard pattern removes ambiguity about what comes next.
Evaluation — 40 submissions received
Total submission count visible at a glance. Publish / Cancel / Reset actions. The educator shifts from creator to reviewer — the AI handles grading structure.
Student evaluation — Aditi Rao (21EC001)
Individual student review: question paper alongside submission. The educator evaluates with full context visible — no switching between screens to cross-reference.
User testing — 25 June 2025

5 sessions. Specific findings. Named changes.

Sessions with educators across subject areas. Each finding had a name, a source quote, and a specific design change attached to it. Testing wasn't validation — it was revision input.

01
The "Generate with AI" vs "Enhance with AI" distinction confused educators

Early testing showed educators didn't understand why some prompts said Generate and others said Enhance. The language implied two different systems. Resolved by unifying under a single "AI Studio" entry point for all generation types.

02
Educators wanted to constrain the AI to their own materials — but couldn't find how

The "Use reference material only" toggle existed but was missed in early versions. Educators in testing actively wanted this feature. Resolved by making the toggle persistent and surfacing it above the fold in the references panel.

03
The Bloom's taxonomy labels on outcomes felt institutional — not useful

Early testing showed educators ignored the Bloom's level column because it felt like compliance overhead. Resolved by keeping the labels but adding a tooltip that explains how the level affects the difficulty of generated assessments — making it feel purposeful.

04
Educators wanted to save mid-session — the Close button felt destructive

In early versions, closing the AI Studio didn't auto-save. Educators who closed accidentally lost their generation. Resolved by auto-saving on close and showing a "Saved to drafts" confirmation, removing the fear of losing work.

05
Educators didn't know AI Preferences were persistent between sessions

AI Preferences (course level, difficulty, theory/application ratio) were set once and remembered. Educators who discovered this reported the most consistent generation quality. Resolved by adding a "Preferences active" indicator in the AI Studio header.

Key design decisions
Decision 01 — Interaction model
One AI Studio for all content types, or a different interface per type?

One AI Studio, consistent across all 10+ content types. The prompt bar, references panel, Close & Accept actions — identical every time. One mental model to learn, regardless of what is being generated.

Decision 02 — Reference control
Should "Use reference material only" be on by default?

Off by default, but persistently surfaced. Making it opt-in respects educators who want broader AI knowledge. Making it visible respects educators who want to constrain it. Both are valid workflows.

Decision 03 — Content versioning
Can educators have multiple versions of the same content type?

Yes — the "Add More" affordance and the naming prompt on save allow multiple versions of Course Outcomes, Modules, and other types. No destructive overwrites. Educators can compare, choose, or combine.

Decision 04 — Compounding AI loop
Should AI-generated content be reusable as AI input?

"Convert to reference" lets educators feed verified outputs back as source material. Course Outcomes inform Modules; Modules inform Lesson Plans. The AI compounds on what the educator has already accepted — not on raw internet data.

Outcome

10+

5+

Every round produced specific, named changes. The testing date is on the prototype — it's a commitment, not a formality.

What I learned
01
AI trust isn't about the AI — it's about the interface around it

The AI on Creator Co-Pilot was capable from day one. The 40% speed improvement didn't come from improving the model — it came from designing the interface so educators felt in control of a powerful tool, not managed by one.

02
Consistency across content types is a design system decision, not just a visual one

Making the AI Studio identical across 10+ content types required resisting the temptation to optimise each type individually. The consistent model made the product learnable. Optimising each type would have made it exhausting.

03
The compounding loop was the product's most interesting design idea

"Convert to reference" changed the product's fundamental model. Instead of using AI once, educators could build a feedback loop where each generation improves the next. That's not just a feature — it's a different relationship with AI authorship.

04
Usability testing on AI tools needs a different lens

Standard testing asks: can users complete tasks? AI UX testing also asks: do users trust what they're seeing, and do they feel in control? Those questions require a different observation protocol — watching for hesitation and doubt, not just errors.
